conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. ___? I’m Dr. ___ from the internal medicine team. I understand you were brought in because your sisters noticed you were confused. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I don’t really remember much. My sisters said I was acting strange, like I didn’t know where I was. I think I even… went to the bathroom in the wrong place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned that too. You were alert when you arrived, but a bit disoriented. We’re trying to figure out why. Do you feel confused now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I feel okay now. Just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We ran some tests. Your CT scan of the head showed no stroke or bleeding. Your labs didn’t show infection either. But we did find something interesting—your urine tested positive for oxycodone and amphetamines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oxycodone? Yeah, I take that for pain. But amphetamines? I’m not doing drugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think you are. Labetalol, one of your blood pressure meds, can sometimes cause a false positive for amphetamines. But the oxycodone is expected. We’re more concerned that your pain meds might be contributing to the confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my pain pills made me confused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Opioids like OxyContin can build up, especially with kidney issues, and affect your brain. That’s called toxic metabolic encephalopathy. Since you’re clearer now, we think lowering your dose helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So I can’t take as much pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll still manage your pain, but more carefully. We’ve reduced your OxyContin from 20 mg twice daily to 10 mg in the morning and 20 mg at night. And your breakthrough oxycodone is now 5 mg every 4 hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my hands and leg? They still hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your wounds. The left leg wound from your recent debridement is healing—good granulation, no infection. Vascular surgery saw you and said it’s stable for now. You’ll follow up with plastic surgery as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my fingers? The dry ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have dry gangrene in a couple fingers due to poor circulation and calciphylaxis. It’s not infected, so no surgery needed now. But we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get really nauseous when I get the sodium thiosulfate. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nausea is common with that infusion. We’ll give you anti-nausea medication before each dose. It’s important you keep getting it for your calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My blood pressure’s been high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been tough to control. You’re on six medications already. We increased your clonidine patch from 0.2 mg to 0.3 mg weekly to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Six? That’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but your kidney disease and diabetes make blood pressure harder to manage. We also held spironolactone for now—it wasn’t helping much and can affect kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my kidney? My last creatinine was going up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your admission creatinine was 2.9, now it’s down to 2.5. That’s improvement. The recent biopsy showed chronic damage from hypertension and diabetes—arteriosclerosis and scarring—but no transplant rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my transplant is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re still on tacrolimus, leflunomide, and prednisone to prevent rejection and manage BK virus. Your levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Slept okay. Still a bit sore, but my head feels clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your mental status is much improved. We think reducing the opioids helped a lot. No signs of infection—blood and urine cultures were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I didn’t have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And your chest X-ray was clear too. So we’re confident it was the medications affecting your brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Me too. We’ll keep monitoring your kidney function and blood pressure. Your transplant team will follow up closely after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs this morning look stable. Creatinine is 2.5, which is better. Blood sugar is a bit high, but we’re managing it with your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to eat less sugar. But with all these meds, it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ll keep adjusting. Your pain is under control with the new doses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, actually. The acetaminophen and lower oxycodone are helping without making me foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s exactly what we wanted. We also stopped gabapentin—it wasn’t helping much and can cause confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I didn’t notice much from it anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is planned for tomorrow. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your meds as we adjusted them. Especially the clonidine patch—now 0.3 mg weekly. Take your sodium thiosulfate with anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—OxyContin 10 mg in the morning, 20 mg at night, and 5 mg oxycodone as needed. Don’t increase it without calling us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my wounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care: daily wet-to-dry dressing on your leg. Apply Santyl ointment as directed. Plastic surgery will see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sisters can help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and home health will assist too. Also, keep all your follow-up appointments—transplant nephrology, vascular, and pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your mental status is clear, blood pressure is better, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Feels good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your instructions with you. Call us if you feel confused again, or if your wound changes, or blood pressure spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.
